description: I’m Rashi, a UIUC graduate (MS AI). I build data and machine learning pipelines in Python. For this challenge I built Vantage, which predicts what a walking astronaut can see along a Mars surface route. It uses 1 m NASA terrain at Gale Crater and the real Curiosity traverse. It flags blind stretches, low sun, steep slopes and a walk-back time that no longer fits a shelter limit. It also works out the fastest way home, where radio contact drops, and where you are from the horizon alone.
summary:
What it is: Vantage predicts what a walking astronaut can see along a Mars surface route. It uses 1 m USGS terrain at Gale Crater and the real Curiosity boxwork traverse, and runs offline in a browser.

How it addresses the challenge: It marks where home, the rover and the suit partner drop out of sight, and it renders the predicted view from the astronaut’s eye height. Slope, hidden ground, low sun and dust roll up into one NOMINAL, CAUTION or HOLD verdict. It maps the fastest way back to shelter and shows where radio contact drops and where a relay fixes it. If the crew is lost, it finds their position from the horizon alone.

Why it matters: On Mars there is no GPS, and the terrain itself hides the landmarks a crew would steer by. I tested the predictions against real Curiosity photos. The horizon fix landed 5 m from the true position on one frame and failed on two, and I report both.
details:
What it does: A browser cockpit for a walking EVA on Curiosity's real route at Gale Crater. A predicted first-person view sits on top, with a map, a visibility strip, a NOMINAL / CAUTION / HOLD verdict and a wrist-style cuff card below. A guided tour shows every feature.

What it contributes

-Position from the horizon alone. Mars has no GPS and no magnetic compass. Vantage matches the skyline a walker sees against predicted skylines at 3,600 places. From one real Curiosity Navcam photo (sol 4748) it found the rover within 5 m of where it stood. It fails on two other photos (far horizon outside the terrain window, too little sky) and says so. NASA Goddard is building horizon navigation for the Moon; Vantage tests it on Mars with a real rover photo.

  • A view checked against reality. Predicted skyline is within 0.43 and 0.63 degrees of real Curiosity photos at two stops, 4.9 degrees low at a third where the horizon is the far crater rim.
  • The way home. Fastest return from the far end is 27 min, against 110 min retracing the route. A "start back within" clock combines shelter limit, daylight and suit time.
  • Radio shadow. Terrain blocks radio to the habitat on 77% of the route; one relay Vantage picks covers all of it.
  • Bad-day checks. Low sun, terrain shadow, slope, hidden ground, partner out of sight, and dust (at optical depth 4, 0.1% of direct sunlight gets through). Each verdict is rechecked within the assumed position error.
  • Onboard assistant interface. An offline MCP server exposes the same checks to any assistant, including one hosted on mission systems.

How it works: USGS 1 m Gale DEM (2.5 km window), line of sight with Mars curvature, skyline grid search with an ambiguity check, Dijkstra for the way home and route planning, geometric sun and Beer-Lambert dust. Validated on 7 Navcam frames at 3 stops with no tuning. Pure JavaScript, no build step, 28 automated tests.

Impact: Planners can compare routes and site habitats and relays; crews get a cuff card and an offline backup position fix. Works for any site with an orbital elevation model. Open source, and every threshold is a labeled, editable assumption.

Limits: Horizons beyond the terrain window are not modeled. The horizon fix assumes heading from a sun sighting and can miss in hollows. Pace and slope limits are lunar planning figures. The shelter check is a time clock, not a radiation model; radio is geometry, not a link budget.

Tools: JavaScript, Python, rasterio, NumPy, Node.js, GitHub Pages and Actions, Model Context Protocol, Claude (Anthropic) for AI assistance.
